newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bank shares pressured by boycott worries.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bank shares pressured by boycott worries.

text.p: Swiss bank shares lost ground on Monday and traders blamed the pressure on renewed discussion of a boycott by world Jewish groups.
Traders said shares in major Swiss banks lost in selling by foreign and Swiss institutional investors.

The selling followed headlines over the latest twist in a long-standing dispute between Jewish groups and Swiss banks over how much money may have been left in Swiss accounts by Jews murdered in the Holocaust.
"This is one reason for investment funds taking their leave from bank shares," one Zurich trader told Reuters.
Traders said concerns had been raised by media reports a boycott of Swiss banks was being considered by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) and Israel's semi-state Jewish Agency.

WJC vice-president Israel Singer and Jewish Agency chairman Avraham Burg told a Jerusalem news conference their organisations were thinking about whether to recommend that Jewish assets be withdrawn from Swiss banks, according to news reports.
"Fear of a boycott is certainly part of the reason (for lower bank shares)," another trader said.
He said there were no other negative rumours on the market that could have prompted the selling pressure.
Another trader said the losses were greater than could be explained by any shift in fundamental economic factors at the banks.
Bearer shares in Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), the country's biggest bank, fell 18 Swiss francs or 1.5 percent to 1,153 francs in early afternoon trade.
Credit Suisse Group, which changed its name from CS Holding as of January 1, was down 1.8 percent or 2.50 francs at 134.
Swiss Bank Corp lost 0.4 percent or one franc to 253.00 Swiss francs.

The idea of a Jewish boycott has been raised several times in recent months as a possible way to force Swiss banks to speed up the hunt for Holocuast accounts or to force the Swiss to set up a compensation fund for hei5rs of Holocuast victims.
The WJC in New YorK said on December 13 it had postponed until late January a decision on whether to urge Jewish money be taken out of Swiss banks.

Swiss diplomat Thomas Borer, who heads a government task force examining whether Swiss banks still hold millions of dollars in unclaimed accounts from Holocaust victims, last month said he thought he had persuaded U.S. congressional leaders not to support any boycott.

The World Jewish Congress, which has been spearheading a battle with Swiss banks over the disposition of Holocaust accounts, has been considering boycott calls from members who are dissatisfed with Swiss efforts to comb bank files for dormant accounts and Nazi loot.
Traders said some investors feared that any boycott could withdraw billions of Swiss francs from the lucrative and growing global asset managment businesses of the big Swiss banks.
